verses.text: When I came to you, brothers, I didn’t come with excellence of speech or of wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of God.
For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling.
My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power,
that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.
We speak wisdom, however, among those who are full grown; yet a wisdom not of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are coming to nothing.
But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden, which God foreordained before the worlds for our glory,
which none of the rulers of this world has known. For had they known it, they wouldn’t have crucified the Lord of glory.
But as it is written, “Things which an eye didn’t see, and an ear didn’t hear, which didn’t enter into the heart of man, these God has prepared for those who love him.”
But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.
For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God, except God’s Spirit.
But we received, not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit which is from God, that we might know the things that were freely given to us by God.
Which things also we speak, not in words which man’s wisdom teaches, but which the Holy Spirit teaches, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things.
Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
But he who is spiritual discerns all things, and he himself is judged by no one.
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?”  But we have Christ’s mind.

footnotes.content: Paul arrives in Corinth—a city wild with eloquence, philosophers shouting on corners, pride running deep. He chooses different. Not 'lesser' precisely, but *other*—testimony over technique. The Lord so often does His best work when we set down our sharpest words.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One name. One death. Paul narrows to nothing else—not circumcision debates or Jewish law or pagan custom, but only Jesus *crucified*. I've found that the deepest wells stay deepest when we don't let a thousand tributaries run in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Weakness. Fear. Trembling. This is the apostle's confession—the man who would plant churches and face mobs and endure shipwreck. He tells Corinth his truth: he came *afraid*. Sometimes the bravest thing is to say so.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not persuasive words—but power. The Spirit at work changes a room in ways rhetoric never can. I've watched this in small ways: one honest prayer moves more than a shelf of arguments. The power Paul speaks of is *real*, not metaphor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your faith resting on human wisdom is like a house built on sand—clever but hollow. When faith roots in God's *power*, it has a foundation that holds through decades, through doubt, through the darkest seasons. That's the difference Paul is naming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The 'rulers of this world' Corinth loved—their philosophies, their status games—all coming to nothing. Paul speaks to those mature enough to hear it: real wisdom doesn't compete with their authority; it outlasts it. A quiet confidence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This wisdom was *hidden*—not secret in the gnostic sense, but kept safe before the worlds were even made. Before you, before me, before creation itself, the Lord ordained your glory in Christ. That predates every earthly plot against your joy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Had they known the *Lord of glory* hung before them, the rulers would have known their own ending. Blindness to Christ is always blindness to reality. The deepest irony: in crucifying Him, they executed their own sentence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah's words echo here: no eye has seen what God has prepared for those who love Him. Not as a vague promise, but as witness to something so true, so vast, that all our earthly sorrow is the prelude to joy we haven't yet imagined.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God *reveals* what He prepared—He doesn't hoard it. The Spirit searches the deep places and brings them to us. This is intimate: God showing His own heart, His own counsel, to ordinary believers. Not a theory. A gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I know my own mind because my own spirit is within me—it's a parable. So with God: His Spirit alone knows His mind. When the Spirit dwells in you, you begin to know what God knows. Not all of it, but *really*—not as guesswork, but as intimate truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not the spirit of the world—its hunger for more, its fear, its endless reaching. But the Spirit from God. He comes to *show* you what has been given to you already: forgiveness, acceptance, a place. Not wages you've earned, but *freely* given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Spirit teaches us to speak—not in the world's polished words, but in words that *match* what we say. Spiritual truths spoken spiritually. Not clever prose, but coherence: your words and the Spirit's breath the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The 'natural man' without the Spirit hears Scripture and sees only foolishness. It sounds upside-down, weak, illogical—because his mind has no equipment to perceive it. Like asking a deaf man to judge a symphony. Discernment is a gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The spiritual person discerns all things—not because he's clever, but because he's been given eyes to see. And strangely: he himself is judged by no one. Not that he's above correction—but the world's measuring stick no longer fits him. He's living by a different measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: 'Who has known the mind of the Lord?' But then Paul answers his own question—*we have Christ's mind*. In His Spirit, we're invited into the very counsel of God, not as distant servants but as those who belong. Even now, that thought steadies me.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
